rewritten_text:
Saturday evenings in our village brought a delightful feeling of having put things in order and taken a peaceful breath before beginning life anew. This encouraged Joe to venture half an hour longer abroad on Saturdays than on other nights. When the extra half-hour and his rum and water had both run out, he rose to leave and took my hand.

“Wait just a moment, Mr. Gargery,” said the stranger. “I believe there's a bright new shilling somewhere in my pocket. If there is, the boy can have it.”

He picked it from a handful of loose coins, wrapped it in a piece of crumpled paper, and handed it over. “Yours!” he said. “Remember! Your very own.”

I thanked him while staring with a rudeness far beyond the limits of good manners and clinging tightly to Joe. He wished Joe good-night, and Mr. Wopsle too, who left with us. For me he had only a glance from his aiming eye—or rather, no glance, since he closed it; but hiding an eye can accomplish wonders.

Had I felt inclined to talk on the journey home, I should have had to supply the whole conversation. Mr. Wopsle left us at the Jolly Bargemen's door, and Joe walked home with his mouth hanging open, trying to wash away the rum with the greatest possible quantity of air. But this reappearance of my former wrongdoing and former acquaintance had left me almost dazed, and I could think of nothing else.

My sister was in no especially ill temper when we entered the kitchen. Encouraged by this uncommon state of affairs, Joe told her of the shining shilling. “A false one, I'll wager,” Mrs. Joe declared triumphantly, “or he wouldn't have given it to the boy! Let me see.”

I unwrapped it, and it turned out to be genuine. “But what's this?” cried Mrs. Joe, dropping the coin and snatching up its wrapping. “Two one-pound notes?”

There were indeed two thick, sweaty one-pound notes, apparently on the closest and warmest terms with every cattle market in the county. Joe seized his hat once more and hurried back to the Jolly Bargemen to return them to their owner. While he was away I settled on my accustomed stool and stared blankly at my sister, quite convinced that the man would no longer be there.

Before long Joe returned. The stranger had gone, he said, but he had left a message at the Three Jolly Bargemen about the notes.

Sir Arnold and Sir Gauter, two knights from the castle, charged against Sir Brandiles and Sir Kay. The four struck each other fiercely, shattering their spears down to their hands. Next Sir Pertolope rode out from the castle to face Sir Lionel. Sir Pertolope, the green knight, knocked down Sir Lionel, Sir Launcelot's brother. Noble heralds watched all this, recording the knights' names and noting who performed best. Then Sir Bleobaris broke his spear against Sir Gareth, but the blow sent Bleobaris himself to the ground. Seeing this, Sir Galihodin warned Gareth to defend himself, and Gareth knocked him down too. Sir Galihud took a spear to avenge his brother, but Gareth treated him the same way. With that single spear Gareth also unhorsed Sir Dinadan, his brother La Cote Male Taile, Sir Sagramore le Disirous, and Sir Dodinas le Savage. King Aswisance of Ireland watched Gareth's exploits and wondered who he could be. On one pass he appeared green, and when he came back he seemed blue. He changed color with every ride back and forth, so neither king nor knight could identify him with any certainty. Then Sir Agwisance, King of Ireland, rode against Gareth, who knocked him from his horse, saddle and all. King Carados of Scotland came next, and Gareth brought down both him and his horse. He did the same to King Uriens of Gore. Sir Bagdemagus then entered, and Gareth struck horse and rider together to the ground. Bagdemagus's son Meliganus broke a spear against Gareth with a powerful, knightly blow. Then the noble prince Sir Galahault called loudly, “Knight of the many colors, you have jousted well! Now prepare yourself to joust against me.” Gareth heard him and took up a great spear. They charged one another, and the prince's spear broke. Gareth struck the left side of his helmet so hard that he swayed from side to side. He would have fallen if his men had not caught him. “Truly,” King Arthur said, “that knight of many colors is a fine knight.” He therefore called Sir Launcelot over and asked him to face the stranger. “Sir,” Launcelot answered, “I am quite willing to leave him alone for now. He has worked hard enough today. When a good knight performs so well, it is no honorable knight's duty to rob him of his glory, especially after seeing how hard he has fought. Perhaps,” Sir Launcelot continued, “his own cause is at stake here today. Perhaps this lady loves him above everyone else present. I can see how he strains and pushes himself to accomplish great deeds. So, as far as I am concerned, he shall have today's honor. Even if it were within my power to take it from him, I would not do so.”

In fairness to the young lady, she did not actually say she would refuse. She merely declared, with great feeling and emphasis, that she would be “blessed” if she agreed. This polite and delicate way of avoiding the request showed the natural good manners of someone who could not bear to hurt another person's feelings with a plain, direct refusal.

The Jewish man's face fell. He turned from this young lady, brightly—even magnificently—dressed in a red gown, green boots, and yellow papers curling her hair, toward the other woman.

“Nancy, my dear,” he said gently, “what do you say?”

“I say it won't work, so there's no point trying to persuade me, Fagin,” Nancy replied.

“What do you mean by that?” Mr. Sikes demanded, looking up sullenly.

“Exactly what I said, Bill,” she answered calmly.

“Why, you're just the person for the job,” Mr. Sikes argued. “Nobody round here knows anything about you.”

“And I don't want them to,” Nancy replied, just as calmly. “So my answer's much nearer no than yes, Bill.”

“She'll go, Fagin,” Sikes said.

“No, she won't, Fagin,” Nancy said.

“Yes, she will, Fagin,” Sikes said.

And Mr. Sikes proved right. By taking turns threatening, promising, and bribing, they finally persuaded her to carry out the errand. Her objections were not the same as those of her pleasant friend. She had recently moved to the Field Lane neighborhood from the distant but respectable suburb of Ratcliffe, so she did not share the same fear of being recognized by one of her many acquaintances.

Miss Nancy therefore prepared to leave, wearing a clean white apron over her gown and hiding her hair-curling papers beneath a straw bonnet. Both apron and bonnet came from Fagin's apparently endless supply of clothing.

“Wait a moment, my dear,” he said, producing a small covered basket. “Carry this in one hand. It makes you look more respectable, my dear.”

“Give her a door key for the other hand, Fagin,” Sikes suggested. “That'll make her look real and genuine.”

“Yes, yes, my dear, it certainly will,” Fagin said, hanging a large front-door key from the first finger of her right hand. “There! Very good! Very good indeed, my dear!” He rubbed his hands together.

“Oh, my brother! My poor, dear, sweet, innocent little brother!” Nancy cried. She burst into tears, twisting the little basket and the door key in desperate distress. “What's happened to him? Where have they taken him? Oh, have pity, gentlemen, and tell me what they've done with the dear boy! Please, gentlemen, please do!”
